previous_description: An ability the product possesses, independent of how it's implemented
definition: An implementation-independent ability the product has or is intended to have, stated as what the product can do (e.g. 'Payment processing', 'Full-text search') rather than as a deliverable unit or a user journey, and realized by one or more features, application components or technology services.

distinguish_from.when: the element is a discrete, user-visible, prioritizable and sizable unit of functionality that ships (e.g. 'Apple Pay checkout button') rather than the enduring ability it contributes to (e.g. 'Payment processing')
the element describes an ordered sequence of user actions toward a goal rather than an ability the product possesses regardless of who uses it or in what order
the element is a single user action or experience at a position within a workflow rather than an ability that many steps may rely on
the element is a dated delivery target that groups capabilities or features rather than an ability itself

code_evidence: a product capability map, roadmap or README section headed 'Capabilities' listing abilities such as 'Search', 'Billing', 'Notifications' that are realized by several features
a top-level domain module, bounded context or service named for a business ability (e.g. billing/, search/, identity/) whose submodules implement several distinct user-facing features

a declared capability set in a manifest or handshake (e.g. a 'capabilities' object in a plugin manifest or protocol initialization response) enumerating abilities the system offers independent of specific UI entry points
notes: Outgoing 'realizes business.businessfunction' inverts ArchiMate, where behaviour realizes capability; consider 'serves' or 'associated-with'. Feature has both 'realizes' and 'uses' toward capability without a stated distinction. A granularity or level attribute (e.g. L1/L2) would help capability hierarchies built via 'aggregates'. Status enum duplicates feature's, blurring lifecycle versus delivery.
